lesson.title: How a mutual fund works
lesson.body:
A mutual fund collects money from many people and invests it in shares, bonds or both. A fund manager makes those choices, and each person owns units of the fund.

The price of one unit is the fund's NAV, worked out from what the fund holds. A higher or lower NAV on its own does not make a fund better or worse. The fund also charges a yearly cost, the expense ratio, which is taken out of the fund's value.

A SIP is one way to buy units: a fixed amount at regular intervals. Funds that hold shares go up and down with the market, so their value can fall as well as rise.
lesson.summary: Many people's money, one fund manager, and units priced by NAV.

terms.title: Mutual fund
terms.brief: A pool of many people's money, run by a fund manager, that holds shares, bonds or both. You own units of the pool.

terms.title: Share (stock)
terms.brief: A small part-ownership of a company. Its price on the exchange moves as buyers and sellers agree on new prices.

terms.title: NAV (net asset value)
terms.brief: The value of one unit of a mutual fund. A higher or lower NAV on its own does not make a fund better or worse.

terms.title: Expense ratio
terms.brief: The yearly fee a mutual fund charges, as a percentage of the money in the fund.

terms.title: SIP (systematic investment plan)
terms.brief: Putting a fixed amount into a mutual fund at regular intervals, such as every month, instead of all at once.
